subject: Floods & Inundation
topic: Global crop loss from compound flood events
summary_contributions: The paper quantifies crop yield loss from compound coastal-fluvial flooding using a coupled hydrodynamic-agronomic model, finding that compound events drive disproportionate losses relative to their frequency. Its key contribution is a globally consistent attribution of yield loss to flood mechanism.
connections_to_my_work: This connects directly to my paper "Severe floods significantly reduce global rice yields", which established the flood-to-yield link at the global scale; the compound-event framing here extends that attribution. It also complements "Societal and environmental interconnections: future directions for flood inundation models" by stress-testing inundation outputs against an agronomic endpoint.
critique_limitations: The agronomic response curves are calibrated on a narrow set of regions, so transfer to monsoon Asia is uncertain. The model also treats drainage recovery as instantaneous, likely underestimating waterlogging duration.
gaps_ideas: A natural gap is the absence of a flashiness dimension — peak rate-of-rise, not just depth, governs crop damage. Pairing this with sub-daily inundation dynamics would sharpen the loss estimates.
advance_disrupt: To advance the field: assimilate Sentinel-1 flood extent and SMAP soil moisture into a daily inundation-stress model, and replace static damage curves with a learned response trained on county-level yield panels. A disruptive step would be a foundation model mapping (rainfall, terrain, drainage) directly to yield loss, bypassing intermediate hydrodynamic simulation.
